description: Single-panel engineering stress-strain plot (six curves, no sub-panels). Ordinate is "Stress /MPa" with major ticks at 0, 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1000; abscissa is "Strain /%" with major ticks at 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100. The legend in the top-right lists six sample labels: LN1 (green dashed), LN2 (grey dashed) and LN3 (orange dashed) for the low-nitrogen steel, and HN1 (grey solid), HN2 (red solid) and HN3 (blue solid) for the high-nitrogen steel. All six curves overlap almost exactly during the initial linear elastic rise, reaching roughly 650 MPa at low strain, then continue on a flat-to-slightly-rising plateau that peaks between the 800 and 900 MPa gridlines. The curves then separate in their falling branch: the LN curves fracture first (LN1 and LN2 drop sharply around 50-55% strain, LN3 near 62% strain), whereas the HN curves extend to noticeably higher strain (HN1/HN2 near 70% and HN3 near 78% strain) and show a long gradual necking descent. Thus the figure demonstrates that nitrogen addition (HN) delays necking and fracture to higher strains while keeping peak stress comparable, i.e. improved plasticity with no loss of strength. No numeric values are printed on the curves; only axis ticks and the legend are legible.

observations.observation: The plot axes are labelled "Stress /MPa" (0 to 1000, ticks every 200) and "Strain /%" (0 to 100, ticks every 20).
Six curves are plotted and identified in the legend as LN1 (green dashed), LN2 (grey dashed), LN3 (orange dashed), HN1 (grey solid), HN2 (red solid) and HN3 (blue solid).
All six curves coincide during the initial steep elastic rise and no clear yield-point drop is visible; they reach a plateau that peaks between the 800 and 900 MPa gridlines.
The falling (necking/fracture) branches separate strongly: the LN dashed curves terminate at lower strain than the HN solid curves.
Among the LN curves, LN1 and LN2 show an abrupt stress drop at roughly 50-55% strain while LN3 extends to about 62% strain before dropping.
The HN curves reach the highest strains: HN1 and HN2 end near 70% strain and HN3 near 78% strain, with a long gradual descending branch characteristic of necking.
The peak stress level is nearly the same for LN and HN groups, so the figure shows nitrogen addition extending ductility rather than raising the maximum stress.
The caption states the figure shows stress-strain curves for the LN and HN steel samples.
The citing text states the UTS values for the low-nitrogen (LN) and high-nitrogen (HN) steels were 832.5 and 841.5 MPa, respectively.

The citing text states the RA and A values of the HN steel were 13% and 12% higher, respectively, than those of the LN steel, and that the YS of the HN steel was significantly lower than that of the LN steel.
The citing text states the LN steel generally broke earlier than the HN steel during local necking, consistent with the earlier fracture termination of the LN curves in the plot.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress-strain curves for six tensile specimens (LN1, LN2, LN3 dashed; HN1, HN2, HN3 solid) plotted as Stress/MPa (0-1000) versus Strain/% (0-100). Curves overlap in the elastic/plateau region peaking between 800 and 900 MPa and diverge in the fracture/necking branch, with HN specimens reaching clearly higher strain than LN specimens.

unreadable_items: No numeric values are printed on the curves themselves; individual UTS/strain values cannot be read from the plot beyond the axis gridlines.
